summary: Describes plans by Computer Corporation of America and the Dynamics Modeling System group at MIT's Project MAC to store data about ARPANET host behavior, collected by a program called SURVEY, in CCA's datacomputer. An interactive program would then retrieve it.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 565 describes a system for saving detailed ARPANET host checks and retrieving selected records later. SURVEY collected the measurements, and SURRET let users query the data stored in CCA's datacomputer.

questions: what was survey on the arpanet
how did survey collect arpanet host data
subtitle: How SURVEY measurements were stored and queried in the datacomputer.

tldr.problem: SURVEY collected detailed information about ARPANET hosts, but kept only a short daily summary and discarded potentially useful details.
tldr.mechanism: The project sent survey records to CCA's datacomputer, which indexed them by host, status, month and year. The SURRET program let users select records by field values or ranges.
tldr.outcome: The described system made detailed survey data available from July 10, 1973, through direct access or SURRET.

today: RFC 565 documents a 1973 system for storing and querying ARPANET host measurements; it says data was available from July 10, 1973, onward.

sections.title: Collecting Host Measurements
sections.content:
Every twenty minutes, the DMS program SURVEY attempted an initial connection to the logger socket of each of 28 network hosts. For each attempt it recorded the date, time, host, status and response time, with response times recorded in tenths of seconds. The status distinguished conditions such as a disconnected host, an unresponsive network control program, a failed or timed-out connection, and an available logger.

When records for all hosts were assembled, SURVEY sent them to CCA's datacomputer. If the datacomputer could not accept them, DMS held the data and sent it again later.
sections.plainLanguage: SURVEY checked each of 28 hosts every twenty minutes and recorded how the check went. If the datacomputer could not accept a set of records, DMS kept it for another attempt.

sections.title: Storing and Finding Records
sections.content:
The datacomputer kept indices organized by host, status, month and year. It could combine these indices using Boolean expressions to select matching records without first examining the stored records themselves. One survey cycle used 17 ASCII characters per host, or 476 characters for the 28 hosts.

SURRET, an interactive program written at DMS in MUDDLE, let a user choose values or ranges for host, date, time, response time and status. The user could ask for any subset of these fields in the result.
sections.plainLanguage: The datacomputer kept separate ways to look up records by host, status and date. SURRET let users choose search conditions and the fields they wanted returned.

sections.title: Making a Query
sections.content:
In the example session, a user selects a host, date and time range, then requests time, status and response-time fields. SURRET turns the request into datalanguage, sends it to the datacomputer and formats the returned records. Users can change criteria and issue another request, or combine host names with Boolean operators.

The RFC says detailed survey data from July 10, 1973, forward was available directly from the datacomputer or through SURRET.
sections.plainLanguage: A user sets conditions such as a host and time range, then requests a result. SURRET sends the query to the datacomputer and presents the matching measurements.
